title: Describing people
goal: Describe what people look like and what they're like, and use possessives.
bekal: describe people with the right adjectives

dialogs.title: Diálogo — La foto de la boda
dialogs.intro: Marta shows a photo from her cousin's wedding and explains who everyone in it is.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Mira, esta es la boda de mi prima Laura.
lines.id: Look, this is my cousin Laura's wedding.
lines.literal: look, this is the wedding of my-cousin(female) Laura.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: ¡Qué guapa! ¿Y quién es el señor alto?
lines.id: She's beautiful! And who's the tall man?
lines.literal: how beautiful! and who is the mister tall?

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Es mi tío Paco, el hermano de mi madre.
lines.id: That's my uncle Paco, my mother's brother.
lines.literal: is my-uncle Paco, the brother of my-mother.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: ¿Y la señora mayor, a la derecha?
lines.id: And the elderly lady on the right?
lines.literal: and the lady older, to the right?

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Mi abuela. Tiene ochenta y siete años, pero está muy bien.
lines.id: My grandmother. She's eighty-seven, but she's doing very well.
lines.literal: my-grandmother. she-has eighty and seven years, but she-is very well.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And the children? Are they your nephew and niece?

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Sí, el rubio es Diego y la morena es Sara.
lines.id: Yes, the blond one is Diego and the dark-haired one is Sara.
lines.literal: yes, the blond is Diego and the dark(female) is Sara.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Diego tiene seis y Sara tiene nueve.
lines.literal: Diego he-has six and Sara she-has nine.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nuestra familia es más pequeña. Solo somos cinco.
lines.id: Our family is smaller. There are only five of us.
lines.literal: our-family is more small. only we-are five.

lines.speaker: Marta:
lines.text: Pero cinco personas también es una familia bonita.
lines.id: But five people is a lovely family too.
lines.literal: but five persons also is a family pretty.

notes: **Adjectives come AFTER the noun.** *El señor alto* (the tall man), *una familia grande*, *un coche rojo*. That's the opposite of English — and beginners almost always slip on the very first sentence.

**Adjectives agree in gender AND number.** *Un niño rubio*, *una niña rubia*, *unos niños rubios*, *unas niñas rubias*. Four forms for one adjective; those ending in -e or a consonant have only two (*grande / grandes*).
**An adjective can stand alone as a noun.** *El rubio* = "the blond one", *la morena* = "the dark-haired one", *los pequeños* = "the little ones". Just put an article in front.
**Mayor** literally means "older", but it's the polite way to refer to elderly people — much gentler than *viejo* ("old"), which sounds rude when used about a person.
**Nuestro has four forms.** Unlike *mi* and *tu*, the word for "our" also agrees in gender: *nuestro coche*, *nuestra familia*, *nuestros hijos*, *nuestras hijas*.
**Está muy bien vs es muy buena.** Health and temporary states use *estar* (*está bien* = she's well / doing fine); permanent qualities use *ser*. This difference is covered in Unit 11.
**Solo = only.** Don't confuse it with *solo* meaning "alone" (*estoy solo*) — same form, context tells them apart.

**Más pequeña** = "smaller". To compare, just put *más* before the adjective and *que* for "than": *más grande que*, *más joven que*. No *-er* endings to worry about. Four adjectives refuse this pattern and have their own forms: *bueno → mejor*, *malo → peor*, *grande → mayor*, *pequeño → menor*.

grammars.title: Possessives — mi, tu, su, nuestro
body: These are the possessives that go **before** the noun. What decides their form is the thing owned, not the owner:
after: Notice *tu* (your) without a ´ and *tú* (you) with one. In writing, the mark is the only difference; in speech they sound exactly the same.

A second way to show possession, always safe from the *su* confusion: **de + owner**. *El hermano de mi madre*, *la casa de Luis*, *el libro del profesor*. When in doubt, use this one — there's no *'s* in Spanish anyway.

blocks.text: Putting it into a sentence: *Mi hermana es alta y muy simpática.* Notice that one *es* is enough for two adjectives joined by *y*.

blocks.title: Family is never far away
items: Sunday lunch with the extended family is still a habit in many Spanish and Latin American families — something nobody needs to arrange because everyone assumes it.
Young Spaniards live with their parents much longer than in northern Europe, often into their thirties. Asking *¿vives con tus padres?* isn't considered nosy at all.

*Mi mujer* literally means "my woman" and is used for "my wife" — normal in Spain, but in some Latin American countries *mi esposa* sounds more polite. For a husband, *mi marido* and *mi esposo* are both safe.
Children are often called by a diminutive: *Juan → Juanito*, *Ana → Anita*, *abuela → abuelita*. The ending *-ito / -ita* adds affection, not just smallness.
Tengo una hermana; ____ hermana es enfermera.
Tengo dos hermanos; ____ hermanos viven en Bandung.
Laura tiene un hijo; ____ hijo tiene seis años.
